 FOCUS REPORT Reversing the Paradigm of VAT Refunds as a Fiscal Threat

Batal Masuk THE government's signal that it regards tax refunds as a fiscal burden has once again ignited a familiar debate. The notion of tightening the disbursement of refunds, and even auditing recipients of large refunds, may reflect fiscal prudence. However, prudence must not become a curtailment of rights.
 Within the value added tax (VAT) system, a refund is not an incentive. It is the logical consequence of a consumption-based tax mechanism. When input VAT exceeds output VAT, as is the case for exporters, for example, the excess is a right that the state must return. Describing it as a fiscal burden risks displacing the fundamental principle of VAT neutrality.
 History has demonstrated that approaches placing excessive emphasis on protecting revenue often give rise to new issues. Indonesia went through a phase of tightened refunds in 1994 as a result of widespread manipulation. Since then, the refund process has been far from straightforward. Audits have been intensified, procedures lengthened and the discretionary powers of the authorities broadened.
 Today, we need to learn from history. Tightened refunds increase the compliance cost for taxpayers. Cash flow is disrupted, administrative costs balloon and business uncertainty rises. In the long run, this can erode competitiveness.
 Moreover, high compliance costs can potentially open the door to misconduct. Tightening procedures without reforming governance will merely shift the issue rather than resolve it. When a process is rife with uncertainty, room for under-the-table negotiation can emerge. That is precisely where the potential for corruption lies hidden.
 The Corruption Eradication Commission ( Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi /KPK in Indonesian) has, in its study , also highlighted a number of systemic issues within the tax authority that could serve as causes of misconduct, including weak refund management and excessively broad discretionary powers.
 The message to the government — specifically to the Ministry of Finance (MoF) in particular — is therefore clear: a VAT refund is a taxpayer's right. Reform should be directed towards strengthening risk-based systems, digitalisation, data integration, and improvements to the integrity of officials. It should not involve a generalised suspicion of refund recipients.
 On the other hand, the stance of Commission XI of the House of Representatives, which has expressed its readiness to collaborate on revising refund regulations, also warrants careful attention. The legislative function is not merely to endorse the wishes of the executive, but to ensure that policy serves the public interest in a balanced manner.
 It must be remembered that the House has constituents: the people, including taxpayers and entrepreneurs. In every regulatory change, meaningful participation is an absolute prerequisite. Transparency, public consultation and adequate academic review must form the foundation.
 A refund is not a matter of the state 'losing' money. More fundamentally, it is a matter of the state returning what was never rightfully its own. In a modern tax system, the speed and certainty of refunds serve as indicators of administrative quality.
 This editorial addresses both branches of power simultaneously. To the executive: do not regard refunds as a fiscal threat. To the legislature: do not neglect the importance of balance and public participation. Tax reform must not move backwards.
 Ultimately, what must be tightened is not the right itself, but the supervision thereof. What must be improved is not the refund, but its governance. In a state governed by the rule of law, a right remains a right, regardless of its value. (sap)
